title: How do you separate CI and CD pipelines in Jenkins (triggers at each stage), and how is Jenkins integrated with a Kubernetes cluster (agents as pods, Kubernetes plugin)?
shortTitle: Separating CI and CD Pipelines in Jenkins and Integrating Jenkins with Kubernetes
keyPoints: The CI pipeline is triggered on every push or pull request and only builds, tests, scans, and publishes an immutable artifact.
The CD pipeline is triggered by CI success or a tag and only deploys the already-built artifact to environments.
Separating CI from CD means the thing tested is exactly the thing deployed, with no rebuild.
The Kubernetes plugin runs Jenkins build agents as ephemeral pods that are created on demand and destroyed after the job.
Pod-based agents give clean isolation, elastic scale, and pinned tool versions for every build.
Use Kaniko or Buildah for image building inside pods instead of mounting the Docker socket.

s1_definition.oneliner: CI builds and certifies an artifact on every push, CD deploys that same artifact when CI passes, and Jenkins runs each build in a throwaway Kubernetes pod.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **CI pipeline** – triggered automatically on every push or pull request; builds, tests, scans, and publishes an immutable artifact to a registry.
- **CD pipeline** – triggered by CI success, a tag, or a manual promotion; takes the already-built artifact and deploys it to an environment.
- **Separation** – CI never deploys and CD never rebuilds, so the thing tested is exactly the thing deployed.
- **Kubernetes plugin** – runs Jenkins build agents as ephemeral pods inside the cluster; each job gets a fresh pod that is destroyed after the build.
- **Pod template** – defines the containers (JNLP, Maven, Kaniko) and resource limits for each agent pod.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India having two assembly lines. The first line (CI) takes raw cheque forms, checks them, and seals them into certified envelopes. The second line (CD) takes only certified envelopes and delivers them to the right branch. For staffing, instead of keeping a hall of permanent clerks, the bank hires a temporary clerk for each batch who appears, does the work, and leaves. In Jenkins-on-Kubernetes terms, each build gets its own pod that spins up, runs the job, and disappears.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In Jenkins I keep continuous integration and continuous delivery as two separate pipelines with different triggers. The CI pipeline is triggered on every push, and its only job is to build, test, scan, and publish a single immutable artifact tagged with the commit SHA. It never deploys. The CD pipeline is triggered by CI success and takes the already-built artifact and promotes it through environments, with a manual approval gate before production.

For build capacity I integrate Jenkins with Kubernetes using the Kubernetes plugin. Instead of permanent build servers, each job gets a fresh ephemeral agent pod that is created on demand and destroyed after the build. This gives clean isolation, elastic parallelism, and pinned tool versions. For image building I use Kaniko instead of mounting the Docker socket, because the socket gives root-equivalent access to the node, which is unacceptable on a shared banking cluster.

The approval gate before production uses the `input` step restricted by `submitter` to named release managers and wrapped in a `timeout`, so an unapproved release aborts rather than hanging forever. Credentials come from the Jenkins credential store or Vault, never from the Jenkinsfile.

Remember one sentence: CI certifies an artifact on every push, CD deploys that same artifact, and Jenkins runs each build in a throwaway Kubernetes pod.
